pool.prompt: A handhole is being placed in a private residential driveway used for daily car traffic. What cover rating is required?
choices: NTC (non-traffic cover) — residential driveways are light-traffic and NTC is sufficient

H-20 — driveways and parking areas with vehicle traffic require an H-20 rated frame and cover (32,000 lb rear axle load class), since even a personal car (2-4 tons) or a delivery vehicle can overload an NTC cover
H-25 — all residential applications require H-25 for future-proofing
No cover rating is required — a plastic lid is acceptable in residential settings
pool.explanation: H-20 is the standard load class for any location subject to vehicle traffic — driveways, parking areas — since NTC covers are only appropriate for yards, unpaved easements, and locations clearly off any vehicle path. A cracked NTC lid in a driveway is both a trip hazard and a permit violation.
pool.citation: AASHTO H-20 load class (32,000 lb rear axle load, 40,000 lb proof load per AASHTO M306), consistent across multiple independent manhole/vault manufacturer technical sources.

pool.prompt: What is the functional difference between a splice handhole and a pull-point handhole?
choices: A splice handhole is man-entry; a pull-point handhole is reach-in only

A splice handhole contains fiber connections and may have splice trays, requiring interior depth for bend-radius transitions and slack coils; a pull-point handhole contains only slack cable with no splices — it exists solely to extend a cable pull and can be sized smaller since it only needs room to coil cable briefly and attach a pulling grip
A pull-point handhole is rated for H-25 traffic loading; a splice handhole always uses an NTC cover
There is no functional difference; the terms are interchangeable
pool.explanation: The distinction drives sizing: a splice handhole needs interior room for bend-radius transitions, splice-tray mounting, and slack coils, while a pull-point handhole only needs room to coil cable briefly and attach a pulling grip — confusing the two leads to either an oversized (wasted cost) or undersized (splice trays don't fit) structure.

pool.prompt: A vault is being sized for a 12-cable splice node (each cable OD 0.75 inches, minimum bend radius = 10x OD = 7.5 inches). What minimum interior dimension is driven by the bend radius, and why?
choices: Minimum interior width must be at least 2 x bend radius = 15 inches — to make a 180-degree turnaround from conduit entry to the splice tray, the cable sweeps through a semicircle requiring the bend radius clearance on both sides of the turn (the actual usable vault interior must exceed 15 inches once cable body and working clearance are added)
Minimum interior depth must be at least the bend radius = 7.5 inches, with no width consideration
Minimum interior width must be at least the bend radius = 7.5 inches for each cable, summed across all 12 cables
Bend radius does not affect vault sizing at all — only cable count and splice tray count matter
pool.explanation: Making a 180-degree turnaround inside a vault (conduit entry to splice-tray working height) requires the interior dimension to accommodate the bend radius clearance through a semicircular sweep — 2 x 7.5 inches = 15 inches minimum for the cable turn alone, with the actual vault interior needing to exceed this once cable body diameter and working clearance are factored in.

pool.prompt: Match each access structure to its primary use case.

items.label: Pull point in a residential utility easement, no vehicle traffic
Slack storage location in a commercial parking lot
Major splice point on a campus backbone route, man-entry required for splice tray work
Network hub node under a primary state highway with heavy truck traffic

pool.explanation: Access structure choice scales with both traffic exposure and function: NTC handholes fit non-traffic easements/yards, H-20 handholes fit vehicle-traffic areas like driveways and parking lots, manholes fit major man-entry splice points, and H-25 vaults fit primary road/highway ROW with the heaviest truck loading.

pool.prompt: The rule of thumb for access structure spacing along a conduit route is 500-1,000 ft. What does this spacing actually optimize?
choices: It ensures conduit fill stays below 40% by providing an intermediate access point to reduce cable count per segment

It keeps required pull tension within the cable's rated maximum by limiting the conduit-run length (and accumulated friction/bends) between pull points — beyond roughly 1,000 ft, bends and friction accumulate enough that a single-end pull frequently exceeds cable-rated tension, so access structures at this spacing allow mid-assist pulls
It satisfies a fixed NESC access-spacing requirement with no engineering rationale beyond code compliance
It ensures the access structures are visible to the 811 locate technician for marking purposes
pool.explanation: This connects directly to the T06.L04 pull-tension principle: the 500-1,000 ft spacing rule exists specifically to manage accumulated pull tension by keeping conduit runs short enough (with mid-assist points available) that a single pull stays within the cable's rated maximum, not for fill-percentage or code-visibility reasons.

pool.prompt: A designer specifies a textbook 1,000-ft spacing for an access structure, but the calculated location falls in the middle of a highway median with no safe construction access. What is the correct design response?
choices: Install the access structure exactly at the 1,000-ft mark regardless of the median location, since the spacing rule is a hard requirement

Move the access structure to the nearest safe, accessible location (e.g., a nearby side street) even if this means the actual spacing is somewhat under 1,000 ft — the spacing rule is a design guideline for tension management, not an exact-location mandate, and constructability/safety take priority over hitting the precise textbook distance
Eliminate the access structure entirely and rely on a single continuous pull for the whole route
Widen the highway median specifically to accommodate the access structure at the calculated location
pool.explanation: The 500-1,000 ft figure is a design guideline driven by pull-tension management, not a precise mandated location — when the calculated spacing point falls somewhere impractical or unsafe (a highway median), the correct response is to move the access structure to the nearest safe, accessible location, accepting a somewhat shorter actual spacing rather than forcing construction into an unsafe or infeasible location.

pool.prompt: A vault design correctly sizes for cable bend radius and includes 12 splice trays for a 12-cable splice node, but is specified with an NTC (non-traffic) cover because 'the vault itself will be buried, only the lid is exposed.' The vault sits at the edge of a commercial parking lot where delivery trucks occasionally cut across the corner. What is the concern?
choices: There is no concern; NTC covers are always sufficient once the vault body itself is properly sized

Cover rating is an independent decision from interior sizing — it depends on the actual traffic exposure at the lid's surface location, not on how well the vault interior was designed; a vault correctly sized inside but under-rated on its cover in a location with any vehicle traffic risk still fails, since the cover (not the vault body) is what bears the surface load
NTC covers are actually MORE load-resistant than H-20 covers, so this design decision is conservative and safe
Cover rating only matters for man-entry manholes, never for smaller vaults
pool.explanation: This reinforces that cover rating (Q1) and interior sizing (Q3) are independent design checks — a vault can be flawlessly sized for its cable/splice requirements while still having an under-rated cover for its actual traffic exposure, since the cover is a separate structural component bearing surface load, and occasional delivery-truck traffic at a parking-lot edge is exactly the kind of exposure that requires H-20, not NTC.

pool.prompt: A designer must choose between a pull-point handhole and a splice handhole at a specific route location where no splicing is planned, only a mid-route cable pull assist. Which is correct, and why does the choice matter beyond just naming convention?
choices: A splice handhole should always be used everywhere, since it can also serve as a pull point with no downside

A pull-point handhole is correct — since no splicing is planned there, the smaller pull-point structure (sized only for cable coiling and a pulling grip, not splice-tray mounting and bend-radius transitions) avoids the unnecessary cost of a larger splice-handhole structure; specifying a splice handhole where only a pull point is needed wastes material and excavation cost for capability that will never be used
The choice has no cost or design implication either way; the two terms describe identical structures
A pull-point handhole is illegal to install anywhere on a route that also contains splice handholes
pool.explanation: This reinforces the Q2 distinction at the design-decision level: choosing the correctly-scoped structure for the actual function needed (pull assist vs. splice point) avoids paying for unused capability — a splice handhole's extra interior depth and splice-tray provisions are real cost drivers that shouldn't be specified where a smaller pull-point structure would fully serve the location's actual purpose.
